Is Pi an inherently endless value, or is it only because we use a Base-Ten numerical system?
What an interesting idea. Never thought of it like this. I hope someone smarter then I can answer this.
Pi can be expressed as an infinite sum of different ratios that are not simple multiples of one another.

Pi is widely believed to be a normal number, meaning that:

is a real number whose infinite sequence of digits in every base b is distributed uniformly in the sense that each of the b digit values has the same natural density 1/b, also all possible b2 pairs of digits are equally likely with density b−2, all b3 triplets of digits equally likely with density b−3, etc. (from wikipedia)

Cool thing about a normal number is that any finite number you can think of exists somewhere in it, and exists in it an infinite number of times. Even if you took all the data on earth and converted it into one really long string of digits, that value would exist in pi an infinite number of times.

Relevant: https://github.com/philipl/pifs

It really helps illustrate how silly copyright law is in a digital world. If every number exists in Pi infinite times, then every song, book, movie, and picture also exist in Pi infinite times. Pi is the ultimate illegal number.

In a base-pi system I suppose it would be 1.
